title: A world in a grain of sand
hookLine: Blake: see a world in a grain of sand
last: A JOY STRONG ENOUGH TO UNSETTLE.

lines: A LITTLE SALT ON A DARK TABLE.
FROM THE STARS TO A GRAIN.
cards: Pour a little salt onto a dark table. Each grain is tiny and rough-edged, easy never to give a second look. The last few days have been about big things: infinite spaces, the starry heavens, the round ocean.
Today a poet points the other way. William Blake begins a poem not with the sky but with the smallest thing on a beach, and says the whole world is in it. Not a picture of the world.

teach.b: Here are the opening lines of Blake's Auguries of Innocence: "To see a World in a Grain of Sand and a Heaven in a Wild Flower, Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand and Eternity in an hour."
Four pairs, each small beside large. First, a world in a grain. Notice the verb: to see.
Blake isn't making a claim about sand. He's describing a way of looking, close enough and long enough that the small thing opens.

teach.h: A HEAVEN IN A WILD FLOWER
teach.b: Second, a heaven in a wild flower. Not a garden rose: a wild one, the kind nobody planted and nobody waters.
Third, infinity in your hand, eternity in an hour. The biggest things there are, set inside a palm and a single hour. Some readers hear a promise that the ordinary day is big enough.

Fourth, the part that's easy to miss: the poem keeps going, in a long run of couplets, and many aren't about beauty at all. They're about harm, to caged birds, starved dogs, hunted hares, and to people too.
The very first: "A Robin Red breast in a Cage puts all Heaven in a Rage." The same seeing that finds heaven in a flower finds heaven's anger at a caged bird.
If a grain holds a world, a small cruelty isn't small either.
The tiny thing is holy, and so the tiny wrong matters.

how: Some people on a personal spiritual path practice close looking at one small object, a seed, a stone, a grain, as a short daily meditation, and Blake's opening lines are often read alongside it.

o: a naturalist who counted the grains of sand along one beach
the poet who saw a world in a grain of sand and heaven in a flower
a monk who copied the Psalms by hand in a small island abbey

games.q: Blake's small and large — tap the pairs.

s: Blake's poem is only about beauty in small things
it goes on to harm: "A Robin Red breast in a Cage puts all Heaven in a Rage."
the opening pairs a wild flower with heaven
the opening lines begin with the verb to see
"To see a World in a Grain of Sand": it's a way of looking.

games.q: Blake has just shown heaven in a wild flower. now he looks at a robin in a cage. what do his next lines say?
o: it puts all heaven in a rage.
it's only a bird; it doesn't matter.
it makes the robin sing more sweetly.
games.why: "A Robin Red breast in a Cage puts all Heaven in a Rage." if a grain holds a world, a small cruelty isn't small.

practice: Put one small thing on your palm or on something dark: a grain of rice, salt or sand, a seed, a crumb of soil. Look only at it, its edges, its color, whether it catches light, and when the mind wanders, bring it back to the grain.
You don't have to see a world; just keep looking, and see what the looking does.

wordCard.voice: Blake. The poet whose way of seeing holds a world in a grain of sand, a heaven in a wild flower, and finds that small harms matter too. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a world in a grain. Blake's way of seeing cuts both ways. I'll be here tomorrow.
